transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-18
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Renee Park (CTO - Opal), Samir Patel (Lead ML Eng - Opal), Lina Gomez (Sec), Jules (PM)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be imperfect):
Opal Telemetry is evaluating Redwood for ingestion + reasoning layer for telemetry parsing and incident triage. Primary constraints: long context (large historic telemetry), multilingual logs (some labels in JP/KO), tool-calling to hit internal search & run queries, and strict compliance (data residency + KMS). They want hosted first for quick POC but may move to Dedicated/Private for residency and audit logs. Interested in 128k context models and tool-calling for enrichment.

Topics discussed:
- Model choices (open models vs license-managed) and perf tradeoffs
- Context length needs and caching (KV cache, prefix caching)
- Tool/function calling and security of tool endpoints
- Deployment options: hosted -> dedicated -> private (VPC)
- Benchmarks, cost modeling, and pilot scope

Action items (captured in notes, see metadata): Maya to send pricing and perf matrix; Diego to propose benchmark; Samir to provide sample dataset.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, this is Diego on the SE side. How's it going?
[00:08] Renee Park: Good thanks. We wanted to run through our needs. We've got a lot of telemetry, like long windows of logs per incident, sometimes 30k to 80k tokens when we include context, um so long context is a big deal.
[00:18] Samir Patel: Yeah and also we have internal tools that the model needs to call — search our vector DB, kick off a run, and retrieve enriched metadata. So function calling support is required.
[00:26] Diego Ruiz: Got it. When you say 30k to 80k tokens, is that per single request or aggregated across candidate documents?
[00:33] Samir Patel: Per incident snapshot. There's a rolling buffer we want the model to see. In some cases the whole history is useful.
[00:39] Jules (PM): Also multi-language bits — we get annotated messages in Japanese and Korean, and sometimes the NL is mixed.
[00:45] Diego Ruiz: Okay that pushes us toward models that have good multilingual capabilities and large context windows — there are a few paths here: Redwood hosted with a high-context open model that we've verified, Redwood Dedicated with a pinned quantized variant for better latency/cost, or on-prem/private if data residency and KMS are hard requirements.
[01:02] Renee Park: Ideally we'd start hosted to move fast for a POC, but we have strict audit requirements for production (SAML, audit logs, KMS).
[01:10] Lina Gomez: Yep, SOC 2 must be included, and we need to know how audit logs look — token-level logs without the payload, and we need to verify KMS integrations.
[01:18] Maya Chen: Totally. We can share our SOC 2 doc and Private deployment brief — also we support customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated. Hosted has envelope encryption with managed KMS, but it's a different control set. I'll send the security brief after the call.
[01:30] Samir Patel: On models, what are you recommending for 128k contexts? We've seen a few vendors doing 64k, 128k, but performance varies.
[01:38] Diego Ruiz: For 128k you usually end up with models that were trained with efficient attention and/or memory optimization. We recommend a two-tier approach: use a 128k-capable model for full incident reconstruction when necessary, and use a shorter context 32-64k variant with aggressive prefix/KV caching for the majority of requests. That reduces cost.
[01:56] Renee Park: What about hallucinations when you're stitching a long history? We can't have false incident conclusions.
[02:02] Diego Ruiz: Great question. You combine retrieval-augmented prompting with certainty checks — we support reranking, tool-calling back to authoritative sources, and can set guardrails. Also model selection matters: some open models have better factuality for system logs. We'll include comparative evals.
[02:18] Jules: Can you name specific open models you think are best fit?
[02:22] Diego Ruiz: Sure — names are a bit messy in the transcript but generally we look at Mistral variants for cost-effective LLMs, Llama 3 family for broad adoption, and some 128k-specialized forks. There are also tuned bifurcations that handle code-like telemetry better. For multilingual, high-parameter multilingual models or finetuned adapters help. We'll send a matrix showing latency, cost, and multilingual scores.
[02:46] Renee Park: Any thoughts on Replicate or Anthropic as competitors? We used Anthropic earlier for some red-teaming.
[02:52] Maya Chen: Customers mention both — Anthropic has strong safety defaults, OpenAI has strong tool ecosystems, Replicate is sometimes used for custom self-hosted models. We'll call those out in the doc.
[03:03] Samir Patel: Tool calling — we need the model to call internal endpoints that can return structured JSON. How does Redwood secure function calls? We don't want open direct network calls from hosted models to our prod APIs.
[03:14] Diego Ruiz: In hosted we recommend using a proxy layer in front of your internal tooling — Redwood's tool-calling offers signed callbacks and allowlist URLs; payloads can be redacted and we support JSON schemas for responses. For Dedicated or Private you can host the tool endpoint inside your VPC and we can do internal routing — that reduces exposure. Also you can enforce RBAC on the tool layer.
[03:38] Lina Gomez: What's the risk of leakage via KV cache or logs? We need to make sure PII from logs isn't retained.
[03:45] Maya Chen: We have configurable retention on KV cache and prefix caching. For Private deployments, you get full control and we can disable cache persistence. For hosted, we have TTLs and redaction options. We'll include specifics in the security brief.
[03:58] Renee Park: Cost — can you ballpark token costs for 128k context runs?
[04:03] Diego Ruiz: Ballpark is tricky, but we'll model scenarios. A single full 128k reconstruction is expensive, so practical designs use retrieval and chunking to keep expensive calls rare. We'll create a cost projection: pure hosted vs dedicated reserved capacity with quantized models.
[04:20] Samir Patel: For the benchmark, we want: accuracy on incident triage, latency under 800ms for short queries, and ability to do a full reconstruction under acceptable SLA (like 3s) when needed. Is that reasonable?
[04:31] Diego Ruiz: That's reasonable. Latency targets depend on model size and hardware; Dedicated with pinned GPU types gives much more predictable p99. Hosted we can hit good medians but p99s are softer. We'll propose a test matrix.
[04:45] Jules: Timeline — we'd like to kick a POC in January and aim for production by March if results are good.
[04:52] Maya Chen: Great, we can try a 2-4 week POC starting in early January. We'll need sample data and success metrics.
[04:58] Renee Park: Ok, next steps?
[05:00] Maya Chen: I'll send the pricing and the model matrix, Diego will send the benchmark plan, Samir will share a small set of redacted telemetry, Lina will list compliance constraints. We'll reconvene after you review.
[05:12] Jules: One question — do you support streaming partial responses? For our UI we want incremental updates.
[05:18] Diego Ruiz: Yes, we support streaming and partial tool-calling hooks, though behavior with very long contexts and streaming can be nuanced — we'll detail that.
[05:27] Samir Patel: Also, does Redwood provide metrics for token-level cost per route? That helps us optimize.
[05:32] Maya Chen: Yep, in Redwood Console you get per-route cost breakdowns, token counts, and tracing. We'll share screenshots.
[05:39] Renee Park: Perfect. Any other risks we should flag?
[05:43] Diego Ruiz: Just to reiterate: for production, data residency and KMS are big decision levers — if you must have keys in your control and network isolation, Dedicated or Private is the right move. Hosted is easiest for POC.
[05:55] Lina Gomez: Noted. We'll review.
[05:58] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. I'll compile notes and send docs.
[06:02] Renee Park: Thank you, appreciate it.

End of call.
